idiom_name: Iterator for streaming parts / LazyList for memoized parts, with lazy val for the shared stage
implementation_notes: Scala's collections offer two staged readers with opposite memory behaviour: Iterator advances through parts on demand and is explicitly not a collection (the documentation stresses that its operations are lazy and that a traversal leaves it at its end, with duplicate available when two consumers must see the same elements), while LazyList is a lazy linked list that computes each element at most once and keeps it - the memoizing choice when the expensive part should be paid once and then re-read cheaply, with the docs warning that retaining the head retains every computed element. lazy val initialises a shared stage on first access, so a common expensive part can be acquired once for all holders. A hand-written plan is still justified when stages must be resumed or validated against an external store rather than against in-memory structure.
code_sketch:
val index: Index = Index.load(path)          // stage 1: cheap metadata
val parts: Iterator[Chunk] =                 // nothing fetched yet
  index.ranges.iterator.map(fetchChunk)      // stage 2: fetched as requested
parts.take(4).foreach(sink.write)            // cost proportional to consumption
pitfalls: An Iterator is single-use and destructive: it is consumed by the first traversal (the collections guide introduces IterableOnce for exactly this split), so a second pass yields nothing unless duplicate or a fresh iterator is used - and duplicate buffers to keep both consumers fed.
LazyList memoizes, which is a feature and a leak: retaining the head retains every computed element, so a streamed resource held in a val grows without bound.
Not every combinator preserves laziness - the LazyList documentation calls out that ++ is eager in its parameter and must not be used to compose lazy lists.
toList/force is a full acquisition hidden behind a standard conversion, and a shared stage in a lazy val has no refresh path once assigned, so invalidation has to be designed around the holder.

variants.name: LazyList for memoized staged elements
variants.idiom_name: LazyList (computes each element at most once)
variants.implementation_notes: LazyList trades memory for repeated acquisition: elements are computed on demand and then held, so a part that is requested again costs nothing while a part that is never requested is never acquired. That makes it the right variant when the same rare part is read several times by different consumers (an index or dictionary that is expensive to decode) and the wrong one for a resource whose parts are large, because a retained head keeps the whole list alive. The documentation is explicit that the laziness depends on construction through #:: and that memoization can leak, so bound the list (take, or a streamed Iterator) when the resource is bigger than memory.
variants.code_sketch:
val index: LazyList[Chunk] =   // elements computed at most once, then held
  LazyList.from(0).map(i => fetchChunk(index0.range(i)))
index.take(4).foreach(sink.write)   // first traversal acquires, later ones reuse
pitfalls: Memoization retains the computed elements: a head reference kept in a val means every part ever requested stays in memory, which is exactly the resource budget the staging was meant to respect.
The laziness is construction-dependent: #:: and #::: build the suspended tail, but many combinators and operations (++ with a strict collection, toList, size) force parts eagerly.
An exception during forcing leaves the partially evaluated list behind, so the holder must be re-created rather than retried in place.
